newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Court ruling unfreezes Montreal airport cons.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Court ruling unfreezes Montreal airport cons.

text.p: The on-again, off-again shift of international passenger flights from Mirabel Airport to Dorval Airport is on again, probably in July, now that an appeals court has swept aside the legal impediments, airline officials said.

A three-judge panel this week overturned a February lower court ruling freezing the shift, as requested by a coalition of Mirabel supporters fearing the ultimate closure of the airport 50 kilometres north of the city.

The shift of scheduled passenger flights to Dorval reverses 22 years of local history and will change the way major airlines serve the Montreal cargo market, leaving freighters and passenger charters at Mirabel while consolidating all other traffic at Dorval.

For Air Canada Cargo, that will mean no longer having to truck some freight each day between its Dorval cargo base and Mirabel warehouse, said marketing manager Gerry Simpson. Air Canada has no freighters.
For Air France Cargo, it means the opposite. Air France will operate passenger flights from Dorval, but freighter traffic will be trucked to and from a Dorval terminal.
Dorval is closer to most Montreal area freight customers, so truck haul time to and from international flights will be shortened, said Simpson.

Because Air Canada operates a Toronto-Dorval passenger shuttle with considerable widebody capacity, it will supplement Toronto's cargo capacity by routing international traffic through Dorval, he said.

That is especially important for Paris traffic, because during the winter schedule, Air Canada's Toronto-Paris service operates 5-6 times a week using Boeing 767 aircraft, while Montreal-Paris always has a Boeing 747 jumbo jet - sometimes even a 747 combi - 365 days a year. From Montreal, Air Canada also flies daily to London.
Many freight forwarders and agents already have beefed up their facilities near Dorval in anticipation of the airport shift.

Mirabel was built in the early 1970s because Dorval - Montreal's only airport for decades - was reaching saturation. Mirabel became Montreal's international gateway, leaving Dorval handling flights within North America. Connecting passengers soon began avoiding Montreal when they found they had to transfer between airports 35 kilometres apart. Several international carriers subsequently stopped flying to Montreal, and the local non-profit airport authority operating both airports says consolidating all scheduled passenger flights at Dorval will help Montreal rebuild its gateway reputation.
Built to handle 12 million passengers a year, Mirabel handles fewer than two million.

Dorval has become even more relevant due to domestic airline deregulation and the Canada-U.S. open skies agreement, signed in 1995. That year, the Canadian government transferred the two airports to the airport authority, which has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into expanding and modernizing Dorval.

Air Canada had planned to service from Dorval to Tel Aviv and Frankfurt this summer, but deferred the launch until 1998 after the February court ruling. Two of the seven weekly Frankfurt flights were to operate through Halifax.
